newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand aims to boost fledgling shipping industry.
newsitem.headline: Thailand aims to boost fledgling shipping industry.

text.p: Thai shipping officials said on Tuesday that new government efforts to boost the fledgling domestic shipping industry were helpful and could prevent outflows of valuable foreign exchange.
But much more was required to develop a solid domestic merchant shipping fleet that could compete effectively with foreign competitors who now dominated business, they said.

The government launched the shipping measures as part of a coordinated effort to narrow the nation's widening current account deficit, which last year stood at a relatively high 8.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
This year, the central bank projects the deficit at around 7.8 percent of GDP, but economists say it may be higher.

Among the measures were an import tariff exemption for purchases of ships larger than 1,000 gross tonnes, income tax reduction on revenue from ship chartering, and tax exemption on revenue from ship sales if proceeds are used to buy new ships.
The Bank of Thailand also set up an eight-billion baht ($315 million) fund to provide soft loans to the maritime sector.
Although export revenues have been Thailand's major growth engine for years, the Thai domestic merchant fleet has missed a number of opportunities to tap the export market.

Freight charges alone paid by Thai exporters to foreign shippers to move their goods to overseas markets in 1995 totalled nearly 20 billion baht (US$800 million), or seven percent of the nation's total payments for services.
"It is extremely good for a start but, still, much more is needed to be done," Sanjay Ambani, Precious Shipping Plc finance director, told Reuters.
Development of human resources, additional tax benefits and rationalisation of merchant shipping laws were needed to make Thailand's merchant fleet more competitive, he said.

The governmment also aims to raise the market share of Thai shipping firms in moving exports to 18 percent in the next five years and to 25 percent in the next 10 years from up to six percent now, according to estimates by industry analysts.

"It's a good start. But the current measures will not be adequate to meet such ambitious targets," said Pruittiporn Nakornchai, an analyst at HG Asia. "And the benefit will not be felt any time soon. It could probably take one to five years."
Complicated ship registration procedures, for example, discouraged shippers from registering their vessels in Thailand, she added.
Thai law stipulates that ships must be present in Thailand to become registered while in some other countries, such as Panama, such regulations were more relaxed, she said.

Precious Shipping's Ambani said that among the additional fiscal measures that the industry needed from the government were corporate tax exemptions for the entire life of vessels and zero value added tax for both inbound and outbound freights.
He was hopeful that any new government, coming in after fresh elections on November 17, would keep the momentum going for the local shipping industry.

"If the target (of increasing market share) is to be achieved, the industry needs to add a 15,000-dead-weight-tonne ship to its fleet every week for the next 10 years," he said. "That cannot be done with current measures alone."
